original_question: For a general Riemannian metric on a sphere of dimension at least 3, and in particular on S^3, does there exist a higher-dimensional extension of Lyusternik and Schnirelmann's theorem guaranteeing multiple closed geodesics?
target_in_paper: §2.1, "Riemannian metrics on spheres" (unnamed open question): "Is there an extension of Lyusternik and Schnirelmann’s result to higher dimensions, in particular to S^3?" ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the paper’s focus on arbitrary Riemannian metrics on spheres of dimension at least 3, singles out S^3 exactly as the paper does, and frames the issue as a higher-dimensional analogue of the classical Lyusternik–Schnirelmann multiplicity phenomenon for closed geodesics on the sphere. ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))
missing_details: The paper’s reference to "Lyusternik and Schnirelmann’s result" is specifically the theorem stated in the surrounding discussion that every Riemannian metric on S^2 has at least three simple closed geodesics; your draft says only "multiple closed geodesics" and omits both "three" and "simple." ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))

The paper does not state a precise higher-dimensional lower bound; it asks only whether any extension of that S^2 theorem exists in higher dimensions, especially for S^3. So a faithful reformulation should not invent a specific number of geodesics in dimension n >= 3. ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))

The scope is arbitrary Riemannian metrics on spheres S^n with n >= 3; no genericity, bumpiness, curvature, symmetry, or nondegeneracy assumptions are imposed. ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))

The surrounding §2 discussion makes clear that the multiplicity issue concerns genuinely different closed geodesics, not merely multiple iterates of one closed geodesic. Your draft leaves that implicit. ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))

For a stand-alone question, it helps to unpack the contrast with the general Lyusternik–Fet theorem: on arbitrary closed manifolds one only knows existence of at least one nontrivial closed geodesic, whereas the open problem asks for a stronger sphere-specific multiplicity statement in higher dimensions. ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))

If the term "simple closed geodesic" is used in the refined question, it should be understood in the standard sense of a closed geodesic without self-intersections; the draft does not indicate this. The paper itself relies on that standard meaning when recalling the S^2 theorem. ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))
refined_question: For every Riemannian metric on S^n with n >= 3, and in particular for every Riemannian metric on S^3, is there a higher-dimensional extension of the Lyusternik–Schnirelmann theorem for S^2—that is, of the theorem that every Riemannian metric on S^2 has at least three simple closed geodesics? ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))
justification: This is the closest paper-faithful sharpening of your draft because §2.1 asks almost exactly this question and nothing broader. The nearby §2 discussion supplies the hidden referent of "Lyusternik and Schnirelmann’s result," namely the three-simple-closed-geodesics theorem on S^2, and also explains that the broader background problem is about multiplicity beyond the one closed geodesic guaranteed on arbitrary closed manifolds. Since the paper does not propose a specific numerical bound or an equivalent reformulation in higher dimensions, the refined question should unpack the S^2 theorem but preserve the open-ended wording "is there an extension" rather than replace it by a stronger invented claim. ([aimath.org](https://aimath.org/pastworkshops/geodesicsproblems.pdf))
